classification.difficultyReason: Explain a general inverse-graph reflection using the square and its diagonals.

content.prompt: The graph of a function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are mirror images of one another in the line $y=x$. The proof of this fact is contained in the image below. How so?

spec.description: Unscaled schematic with positive axis arrowheads, an ascending diagonal through the origin, two reflected increasing curves, and an axis-aligned square with both diagonals and all four corner labels. Control coordinates determine only the schematic appearance and are not numerical givens or asserted curve equations.
spec.mathematics: The square has corners (a,a), (a,b), (b,b), (b,a). Its diagonal from (a,a) to (b,b) lies on y=x and perpendicularly bisects the segment joining (a,b) and (b,a). The orange curve is obtained by exchanging the coordinates of every point on the blue curve.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied geometry and labels remain visible in the question; no solution-only annotations are added.

answer.short:
The line $y=x$ is the perpendicular bisector of the diagonal joining $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$, so these points are reflections of one another.

An inverse exchanges the coordinates of every point, so the two graphs are mirror images in $y=x$.
answer.worked:
If $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $f$, then $f(a)=b$, so $f^{-1}(b)=a$ and $(b,a)$ lies on the graph of $f^{-1}$.

The indicated quadrilateral is a square: its sides are horizontal or vertical and have equal length $|b-a|$. Its diagonals bisect one another at right angles. The diagonal joining $(a,a)$ and $(b,b)$ lies on $y=x$, so $y=x$ perpendicularly bisects the other diagonal, joining $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$.

Therefore $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ are reflections in $y=x$. This holds for every point on the graph; points with $a=b$ remain on the reflection line. Hence the graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are mirror images in $y=x$.
